prompt: As seen in the diagram, three darts are thrown at nine fixed balloons. If a balloon is hit, it bursts and the dart continues in the same direction it had before. How many balloons will **not** be hit by a dart?

solutions.title: Follow each dart
solutions.body:
Each dart flies straight to the right along its dashed line. A balloon is hit if the line passes through it.
- **Top dart:** passes through the grey balloon on the left and the big dark balloon on the right → 2 balloons.
- **Middle dart:** passes through the tiny white balloon and the big black balloon on the far right → 2 balloons.
- **Bottom dart:** passes through the big white balloon and the small dark balloon → 2 balloons.

That is $2 + 2 + 2 = 6$ balloons hit, so $9 - 6 = 3$ are not hit.

**Answer: (B) 3**

solutions.title: Look for the safe balloons
solutions.body:
Instead, look for balloons that lie completely *between* the darts' lines:
- the big dark balloon in the upper middle (it sits below the top line and above the middle line),
- the small black balloon at the top (also between the top and middle lines),
- the grey balloon at the lower right (between the middle and bottom lines).

Those 3 balloons are never touched.

**Answer: (B) 3**

prompt: Peter places three building blocks on a table, as shown. What does he see when he is looking at them from above?

solutions.title: Place each block from above
solutions.body:
From above, every block becomes a flat shape:
- the long block becomes a long rectangle,
- the cube (at the right end, sticking out to the back) becomes a small square **above** the right end of the rectangle,
- the cylinder (standing in front of the long block, about one third of the way from the left) becomes a circle **below** the rectangle, about one third from the left.

Only picture (C) has the square at the right end and the circle about a third of the way along.

**Answer: (C)**

solutions.title: Rule out wrong pictures
solutions.body:
- The cube is at the **right** end, so (D) and (E) (square on the left) are wrong.
- The cylinder is not at the far right end and not at the far left end, so (A) (circle at the right end) and (B) (circle at the left end) are wrong.

Only (C) is left.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: If you hit the target board, you score points. The number of points depends on which one of the three areas you hit. Diana throws two darts, three times, at the target board. On the first attempt she scores 14 points and on the second 16 points. How many points does she score on the third attempt?

solutions.title: Find each area's value
solutions.body:
- First attempt: both darts are in the light ring. So one light ring is worth $14 \div 2 = 7$ points.
- Second attempt: one dart in the light ring and one in the centre: $7 + \text{centre} = 16$, so the centre is worth $9$.
- Third attempt: both darts are in the centre: $9 + 9 = 18$.

**Answer: (B) 18**

solutions.title: Swap one dart at a time
solutions.body:
Going from attempt 1 to attempt 2, one dart moves from the light ring into the centre and the score goes up by $16 - 14 = 2$.

Going from attempt 2 to attempt 3, the *other* dart makes the same move (light ring → centre), so the score goes up by 2 again: $16 + 2 = 18$.

**Answer: (B) 18**

prompt: A garden is split into equally sized square lots, each 1 m wide. A fast snail and a slow snail crawl in different directions along the outside edge of the garden. Both start at corner S. The slow snail crawls 1 m in one hour and the fast one crawls 2 m in one hour. At which position will the two snails meet for the first time?

solutions.title: Share the distance
solutions.body:
The garden is 10 squares long and 2 squares wide, so the edge all the way around is $10 + 2 + 10 + 2 = 24$ m.

Together the snails crawl $1 + 2 = 3$ m every hour, so they meet after $24 \div 3 = 8$ hours.

In 8 hours the slow snail crawls 8 m: 2 m up the left side, then 6 m to the right along the top. That is 6 squares from the left on the top edge, which is point **B**.

**Answer: (B) B**

solutions.title: Check with the fast snail
solutions.body:
In 8 hours the fast snail crawls $16$ m: 10 m along the bottom, 2 m up the right side, then 4 m back to the left along the top.

The top edge is 10 m long, so it ends up $10 - 4 = 6$ m from the left corner. A is 5 m, B is 6 m and C is 7 m from the left, so they meet at B.

**Answer: (B) B**

prompt: A star consists of a square and four triangles. All sides of the triangles are equally long. The perimeter of the square is 36 cm. What is the perimeter of the star?

solutions.title: Count the outside edges
solutions.body:
The square's side is $36 \div 4 = 9$ cm. Each triangle shares one side with the square, so all triangle sides are 9 cm.

Around the outside of the star, each triangle shows 2 sides: $4 \times 2 = 8$ sides of 9 cm.

$8 \times 9 = 72$ cm.

**Answer: (E) 72 cm**

solutions.title: Double the square
solutions.body:
Each side of the square is replaced on the outside by **two** sides of a triangle, each as long as the square's side. So the outside path is exactly twice as long as the square's perimeter: $2 \times 36 = 72$ cm.

**Answer: (E) 72 cm**

prompt: A big spot of ink covers most of a calendar page of a certain month. Which day of the week does the 25th day of that month fall on? (The calendar uses German day names: Mo = Monday, Di = Tuesday, Mi = Wednesday, Do = Thursday, Fr = Friday, Sa = Saturday, So = Sunday.)

solutions.title: Jump by weeks
solutions.body:
The 2nd is in the Do column, so the 2nd is a **Thursday**.

Adding 7 days keeps the same weekday: the 9th, 16th and 23rd are also Thursdays.

Then the 24th is Friday and the 25th is **Saturday**.

**Answer: (D) Saturday**

solutions.title: Use remainders
solutions.body:
The 2nd is a Thursday. From the 2nd to the 25th is $25 - 2 = 23$ days.

$23 = 3 \times 7 + 2$, so after 3 whole weeks we move 2 more days: Thursday → Friday → **Saturday**.

**Answer: (D) Saturday**

prompt: How many times do you have to roll an ordinary die in order to be certain that at least one number is rolled twice?

solutions.title: Think about the unluckiest case
solutions.body:
A die has 6 different numbers. With bad luck, the first 6 rolls could all be different: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

The 7th roll **must** repeat one of them, because there are no new numbers left.

So 6 rolls are not enough, but 7 rolls always are.

**Answer: (C) 7**

solutions.title: Boxes and balls
solutions.body:
Imagine 6 boxes, one for each number. Each roll puts a ball into a box.

With 6 balls you could put one in each box. With 7 balls, some box must get 2 balls — that number was rolled twice.

**Answer: (C) 7**

prompt: A figure is made up of three squares. The side length of the smallest square is 6 cm. How long is the side length of the biggest square?

solutions.title: Medium square first
solutions.body:
- The medium square (top left) is 2 cm taller than the small square: $6 + 2 = 8$ cm.
- Along the top, the medium and small squares together are $8 + 6 = 14$ cm wide.
- The big square is 2 cm narrower than that: $14 - 2 = 12$ cm.

**Answer: (C) 12 cm**

solutions.title: Check with the lengths
solutions.body:
If the big square were 12 cm, then the medium square (8 cm) plus the small square (6 cm) would stick out $8 + 6 - 12 = 2$ cm on the right — exactly the 2 cm shown in the picture. ✓

**Answer: (C) 12 cm**

prompt: Alice subtracts one two-digit number from another two-digit number. Afterwards she paints over two digits in the calculation, as shown. What is the sum of the two painted digits?

solutions.title: Ones digits first
solutions.body:
The calculation is $\square 3 - 2\square = 25$.

Ones: $3 - \square$ must end in 5. That only works with borrowing: $13 - 8 = 5$. So the second hidden digit is **8**.

Now $\square 3 - 28 = 25$, so $\square 3 = 25 + 28 = 53$. The first hidden digit is **5**.

Sum: $5 + 8 = 13$.

**Answer: (D) 13**

solutions.title: Turn it into addition
solutions.body:
Subtraction can be checked by adding: $25 + 2\square = \square 3$.

Ones: $5 + \square$ ends in 3, so $\square = 8$ ($5 + 8 = 13$, carry 1).

Tens: $2 + 2 + 1 = 5$, so the other digit is 5. Check: $53 - 28 = 25$ ✓.

Sum: $5 + 8 = 13$.

**Answer: (D) 13**

prompt: In the diagram the circles represent light bulbs, which are connected to some other light bulbs. Initially all light bulbs are switched off. If you touch a light bulb, then that light bulb and all directly connected light bulbs switch on. What is the minimum number of light bulbs you have to touch in order to switch on all the light bulbs?

solutions.title: Find two good bulbs
solutions.body:
There are 8 bulbs.
- Touch the **bottom-right** bulb: it switches on itself, the bottom-left bulb, the right-hand bulb and the bulb next to it in the middle — 4 bulbs.
- Touch the **upper bulb of the small left triangle** (the one joined to the top bulb): it switches on itself, the top bulb and the other two bulbs of the small triangle — 4 more bulbs.

$4 + 4 = 8$, so all bulbs are on after just 2 touches.

**Answer: (A) 2**

solutions.title: Why 1 is not enough
solutions.body:
No bulb is connected to more than 3 others, so one touch switches on at most $1 + 3 = 4$ bulbs. There are 8 bulbs, so we need at least 2 touches.

And 2 touches are enough (bottom-right bulb plus the top bulb of the small triangle, which together cover all 8).

**Answer: (A) 2**

prompt: Four equally big squares are partially coloured black. In which of the four squares is the total area of the black parts biggest?

choices.text: The total area of the black parts is always equally big.

solutions.title: Compare with a quarter
solutions.body:
- **A:** one quarter of the square is black → $\frac{1}{4}$.
- **B:** two triangles, each half of a quarter-square → $\frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{4}$.
- **C:** the lines cut each quarter-square into 4 small triangles ($\frac{1}{16}$ each). Each black diamond is 2 small triangles, so 2 diamonds = 4 small triangles = $\frac{4}{16} = \frac{1}{4}$.
- **D:** 4 black small triangles, each $\frac{1}{16}$ → $\frac{4}{16} = \frac{1}{4}$.

They are all the same!

**Answer: (E) The total area of the black parts is always equally big.**

solutions.title: Cut and move pieces
solutions.body:
In B, slide the lower black triangle up next to the upper one: together they fill one quarter-square, just like A.

In C and D, each black piece is made of small triangles that are $\frac{1}{4}$ of a quarter-square. There are 4 such small triangles in each picture, so again they fill exactly one quarter-square.

So every square is one quarter black.

**Answer: (E) The total area of the black parts is always equally big.**

prompt: The four smudges hide four of the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The calculations along the two arrows are correct. Which number is hidden behind the smudge with the star?

solutions.title: Start with the harder path
solutions.body:
Call the smudges: left $L$, star $S$, right $R$, bottom $B$.

The paths say $L + S - R = 8$ and $L \times B \div R = 8$.

For the second one, $L \times B = 8 \times R$. With different numbers from 1 to 5, the only possibility is $R = 1$ and $L \times B = 8$, so $L$ and $B$ are 2 and 4.

Then $L + S - 1 = 8$, so $L + S = 9$. If $L = 2$, $S = 7$ (impossible). So $L = 4$ and $S = 5$.

**Answer: (E) 5**

solutions.title: Try the answer choices
solutions.body:
The top path needs $L + S = 8 + R$, which is at least 9. Two different numbers up to 5 can only reach 9 as $4 + 5$, so $R = 1$ and $\{L, S\} = \{4, 5\}$.

Now the bottom path: $L \times B \div 1 = 8$. If $L = 5$, then $B$ is not a whole number. So $L = 4$, $B = 2$, and the star is $S = 5$.

Check: $4 + 5 - 1 = 8$ ✓, $4 \times 2 \div 1 = 8$ ✓.

**Answer: (E) 5**

prompt: A lion hides in one of three rooms. On the door to room number 1 a note reads: "The lion is not here." On the door to room number 2 a note reads: "The lion is here." On the door to room number 3 a note reads: "$2 + 3 = 5$." Exactly one of the three notes is true. In which room is the lion?

choices.text: It can be in any room.
It is either in room 1 or room 2.

solutions.title: Use the true note
solutions.body:
The note on room 3 says $2 + 3 = 5$, which is **always true**. Since exactly one note is true, the other two notes must be false.

- Room 1's note "The lion is not here" is false → the lion **is** in room 1.
- Room 2's note "The lion is here" is false → the lion is not in room 2. ✓

**Answer: (A) Room 1**

solutions.title: Test each room
solutions.body:
Count the true notes for each possible room:
- Lion in room 1: notes are false, false, true → 1 true ✓
- Lion in room 2: true, true, true → 3 true ✗
- Lion in room 3: true, false, true → 2 true ✗

Only room 1 works.

**Answer: (A) Room 1**

prompt: Two girls, Eva and Olga, and three boys, Adam, Isaac and Urban, play together with a ball. If a girl has the ball, she throws it either to the other girl or to a boy. Every boy only throws the ball to another boy, but not to the one the ball has just come from. The first throw is made by Eva to Adam. Who makes the 5th throw?

solutions.title: Follow the ball
solutions.body:
- Throw 1: Eva → Adam.
- Throw 2: Adam must throw to a boy: Isaac or Urban. Say Isaac.
- Throw 3: Isaac can't throw back to Adam, so Isaac → Urban.
- Throw 4: Urban can't throw back to Isaac, so Urban → Adam.
- Throw 5: **Adam** throws.

If Adam had thrown to Urban instead, it goes Urban → Isaac → Adam — again Adam makes throw 5.

**Answer: (A) Adam**

solutions.title: Spot the circle
solutions.body:
Once a boy has the ball, it never goes back to the girls, and it can't go back to where it came from. So the three boys pass it **around in a circle**: Adam → one boy → the other boy → Adam → …

Adam throws number 2, and every 3 throws the ball is back with him: throws 2, 5, 8, … So Adam makes throw 5.

**Answer: (A) Adam**

prompt: The faces of a die are either white, grey or black. Opposite faces are always a different colour. Which of the following nets does **not** belong to such a die?

solutions.title: Find the opposite pairs
solutions.body:
In a net with a row of 4 squares, the 1st and 3rd squares are opposite, the 2nd and 4th are opposite, and the square above the row is opposite the square below the row.

Check net (E): the row is grey, black, black, grey. 1st & 3rd: grey/black ✓. 2nd & 4th: black/grey ✓. But the square above (white) and the square below (white) are opposite and **both white** ✗.

All the other nets have three pairs of different colours.

**Answer: (E)**

solutions.title: Fold it in your head
solutions.body:
Fold net (E): the row of four wraps around to make the sides. The white square on top folds over to become the lid, and the white square at the bottom folds under to become the base. Lid and base are opposite, and both are white — not allowed.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: From the list of numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, Monika chooses 3 different numbers whose sum is 8. From the same list Daniel chooses 3 different numbers whose sum is 7. How many of the numbers were chosen by both Monika and Daniel?

solutions.title: List all possibilities
solutions.body:
- Three different numbers with sum 7: only $1 + 2 + 4$. So Daniel has {1, 2, 4}.
- Three different numbers with sum 8: $1 + 2 + 5$ or $1 + 3 + 4$.

Compare with {1, 2, 4}:
- {1, 2, 5} shares 1 and 2 → 2 numbers.
- {1, 3, 4} shares 1 and 4 → 2 numbers.

Either way, 2 numbers are shared.

**Answer: (C) 2**

solutions.title: Small numbers only
solutions.body:
The smallest three numbers already add to $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$, so both children must use very small numbers. Both must contain the 1 (without it, the smallest sum is $2 + 3 + 4 = 9$).

Daniel: {1, 2, 4}. Monika: {1, 2, 5} or {1, 3, 4}. In each case, exactly one more number besides 1 is shared, giving 2 in total.

**Answer: (C) 2**

prompt: Emily wants to write a number into every empty small triangle. The sum of the numbers in any two triangles with a common side should always be the same. Two numbers are already given. What is the sum of all the numbers in the figure?

solutions.title: Neighbours of the same triangle are equal
solutions.body:
If one triangle touches two others, both pairs have the same sum, so those two others must hold the **same number**.

Because of this, all the triangles pointing **up** get the same number, and all the triangles pointing **down** get the same number.

- The 2 is in an up-triangle, so all 6 up-triangles hold 2: $6 \times 2 = 12$.
- The 3 is in a down-triangle, so all 3 down-triangles hold 3: $3 \times 3 = 9$.

Total: $12 + 9 = 21$.

**Answer: (C) 21**

solutions.title: Fill it in
solutions.body:
Every pair of neighbours must add to the same total. The 2 and the 3 are not neighbours, but try putting 3 in every down-triangle and 2 in every up-triangle: every shared side is between an up- and a down-triangle, so every pair adds to $2 + 3 = 5$ ✓.

Count: 6 up-triangles and 3 down-triangles. Sum $= 6 \times 2 + 3 \times 3 = 21$.

**Answer: (C) 21**

prompt: Instead of digits, Hannes uses the letters A, B, C and D in a calculation, as shown. Different letters stand for different digits. Which digit does the letter B stand for?

solutions.title: Find D first
solutions.body:
$ABC + CBA = DDDD$. Two three-digit numbers add up to less than 2000, so $DDDD = 1111$.

- Ones: $C + A$ ends in 1, so $C + A = 11$ (carry 1).
- Tens: $B + B + 1$ must end in 1, so $B + B$ ends in 0: $B = 0$ or $B = 5$.
- If $B = 5$: tens give $11$, carry 1, and then hundreds give $A + C + 1 = 12$ — that would end in 2, not 1 ✗.
- If $B = 0$: tens give 1, no carry; hundreds give $A + C = 11$ → 1, carry 1 → 1111 ✓.

So $B = 0$. (Example: $209 + 902 = 1111$.)

**Answer: (A) 0**

solutions.title: Test the choices
solutions.body:
We need $ABC + CBA = 1111$ with $A + C = 11$ (to make the ones digit 1).

Try $B = 0$ with $A = 2, C = 9$: $209 + 902 = 1111$ ✓.

Try $B = 5$: $259 + 952 = 1211$ ✗. Any other $B$ (2, 4, 6) makes the tens digit $2B + 1$ not end in 1 ✗.

**Answer: (A) 0**

prompt: Four ladybirds each sit on a different cell of a 4 × 4 grid. One is asleep and does not move. On each whistle, the other three each move to an adjacent free cell. They can crawl up, down, right or left, but are never allowed to move back to the cell they have just come from. The pictures show the initial position and the positions after the first, second and third whistles. Where could the ladybirds be after the fourth whistle?

solutions.title: Find the sleeper, then the moves
solutions.body:
The ladybird in row 3, column 2 never moves — it is asleep.

After the third whistle the others are at: row 2 col 2 (came from above), row 2 col 4 (came from below), row 4 col 3 (came from the left).

Where can each go next (not back, not onto the sleeper)?
- row 2 col 2 → left (row 2 col 1) or right (row 2 col 3)
- row 2 col 4 → up (row 1 col 4) or left (row 2 col 3)
- row 4 col 3 → right (row 4 col 4) or up (row 3 col 3)

Picture (A) has the sleeper plus row 2 col 1, row 1 col 4 and row 3 col 3 — all allowed moves ✓.

**Answer: (A)**

solutions.title: Rule out the others
solutions.body:
- (E): the sleeper's cell (row 3, col 2) is empty — impossible.
- (C): there is a ladybird in the top-left corner, which no ladybird can reach in one step.
- (B): a ladybird is at row 3 col 4, which no ladybird can reach.
- (D): the bottom ladybird (row 4 col 3) must move to row 4 col 4 or row 3 col 3, but neither cell is occupied in (D).

Only (A) is possible.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: The five balls weigh 30 g, 50 g, 50 g, 50 g and 80 g. Which of the balls weighs 30 g?

solutions.title: Start with the balanced scale
solutions.body:
All balls together weigh $30 + 50 + 50 + 50 + 80 = 260$ g. The right-hand scale is balanced: $A + D = B + C + E = 130$ g. Two balls can only make 130 as $80 + 50$, so A and D are 80 g and 50 g.

- If $A = 80$: the middle scale says $E + B$ is heavier than $A + C$, but $E + B$ is at most $50 + 50 = 100$, while $A + C$ is at least 110 ✗.
- So $D = 80$ and $A = 50$. Now the middle scale says $E + B > 50 + C$. If C were 50 we would need $E + B > 100$ — impossible. So **C = 30 g**.

Check the left scale: $C + D = 110 > A + B = 100$ ✓.

**Answer: (C) C**

solutions.title: Test each ball as the 30 g ball
solutions.body:
A and D share 130 g, so they are 80 and 50; the 30 g ball is B, C or E.
- **B = 30:** then C and E are 50 each. Middle scale: $E + B = 80$ should be heavier than $A + C \ge 100$ ✗.
- **E = 30:** then B and C are 50 each. Middle scale: $E + B = 80$ vs $A + C \ge 100$ ✗.
- **C = 30:** B and E are 50. Middle scale: $100 > A + 30$ needs $A = 50$, so $D = 80$. Left scale: $30 + 80 = 110 > 50 + 50 = 100$ ✓.

**Answer: (C) C**

prompt: Three different digits A, B and C are chosen. Then the biggest possible six-digit number is built in which the digit A appears 3 times, the digit B 2 times and the digit C 1 time. Which representation is definitely **not** possible for this number?

solutions.title: Biggest means digits go down
solutions.body:
To make the biggest number, you put the largest digit first, then the next largest, and so on. So equal digits sit **together** and the digits never go up from left to right.

In AAABCB the two B's are separated by C. That would need $B > C$ (B before C) **and** $C > B$ (C before the last B) — impossible.

All other choices fit some order: AAABBC ($A>B>C$), CAAABB ($C>A>B$), BBAAAC ($B>A>C$), AAACBB ($A>C>B$).

**Answer: (D) AAABCB**

solutions.title: Try real digits
solutions.body:
Pick digits for the other choices: e.g. A = 9, B = 5, C = 1 gives 999551 = AAABBC ✓; C = 9, A = 5, B = 1 gives 955511 = CAAABB ✓; and so on.

For AAABCB: look at the last three digits B, C, B.
- If $B > C$, then AAABBC is bigger (e.g. 999515 < 999551).
- If $C > B$, then AAACBB is bigger (e.g. 999191 < 999911).

Either way there is a bigger number with the same digits, so AAABCB is never the biggest.

**Answer: (D) AAABCB**

prompt: The sum of Kathi's age and her mother's age is 36. The sum of her mother's age and her grandmother's age is 81. How old was Kathi's grandmother when Kathi was born?

solutions.title: Compare the two sums
solutions.body:
- Kathi + Mother = 36
- Mother + Grandmother = 81

Both sums contain the mother. So the difference $81 - 36 = 45$ is exactly how much older Grandmother is than Kathi.

When Kathi was born (age 0), Grandmother was 45.

**Answer: (C) 45**

solutions.title: Try an example
solutions.body:
Pick any age for Kathi, e.g. 6. Then Mother is $36 - 6 = 30$, and Grandmother is $81 - 30 = 51$.

Grandmother is $51 - 6 = 45$ years older than Kathi, so she was 45 when Kathi was born. (Any other choice for Kathi's age gives the same difference.)

**Answer: (C) 45**

prompt: Nick wants to split the numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 into some groups so that the sum of the numbers in each group is the same. What is the largest number of groups he can make?

solutions.title: Total and group sum
solutions.body:
Total: $2 + 3 + \dots + 10 = 54$.

The group containing 10 has a sum of at least 10. The group sum must divide 54 evenly. Divisors of 54 that are at least 10: 18, 27, 54. The smallest is 18, which gives $54 \div 18 = 3$ groups.

It works: $\{10, 8\}$, $\{9, 7, 2\}$, $\{6, 5, 4, 3\}$ — each sums to 18.

**Answer: (B) 3**

solutions.title: Why not more groups?
solutions.body:
- 4 groups: $54 \div 4$ is not a whole number ✗.
- 6 groups: each would sum to $54 \div 6 = 9$, but then the 10 can't fit in any group ✗.
- More groups make the sum even smaller ✗.

3 groups of 18 work (e.g. 10+8, 9+7+2, 6+5+4+3), so 3 is the most.

**Answer: (B) 3**

prompt: The figure shown consists of one square part and eight rectangular parts. Each part is 8 cm wide. Peter puts all the parts together to form one long rectangle that is 8 cm wide. How long is this rectangle?

solutions.title: Use the area
solutions.body:
Across the big square there are 5 strips of width 8 cm (outer strip, inner strip, centre, inner strip, outer strip), so the big square is $5 \times 8 = 40$ cm on each side.

Its area is $40 \times 40 = 1600$ cm². The long rectangle has the same area and is 8 cm wide, so its length is $1600 \div 8 = 200$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 200 cm**

solutions.title: Add up the pieces
solutions.body:
Measure in 8 cm units. The big square is 5 units wide.
- Outer ring: 4 rectangles, each 4 units long → 16 units.
- Inner ring: 4 rectangles, each 2 units long → 8 units.
- Centre square: 1 unit.

Laid end to end: $16 + 8 + 1 = 25$ units $= 25 \times 8 = 200$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 200 cm**
